tip: A modal like 'kann' pushes the main verb to the very end as an infinitive: 'kann heute nicht kommen'.
For things, not people, German fuses 'da-' ('dar-' before a vowel) with a preposition: 'darüber' means about it, standing for 'über' plus it.
German says to have fear rather than to be afraid: 'Angst haben vor', as in 'Angst vor Spinnen'.
Many verbs with 'a' in the stem take an umlaut in the 'er/sie' form: 'vergraben' becomes 'vergräbt', buries.
'Schulden' means debts and is normally plural only; the singular 'Schuld' means guilt or fault instead.
'Bescheid bekommen' is a set phrase meaning to get word or be informed; 'Bescheid' stays capitalized and unchanged.
Add '-d' to a verb to use it like an adjective: 'schnurren' gives 'schnurrend', purring; here it takes the adjective ending in 'schnurrenden'.
The pronoun 'niemand' takes case endings like an article; the dative object here is 'niemandem', meaning to nobody.
A few countries carry an article: 'die Schweiz'. To say in it, use the dative: 'in der Schweiz'.
The verb 'sich beschweren' means to complain; the 'sich' is required, as in 'hat sich beschwert'.
Here 'davon' fuses 'da-' with 'von', the preposition that goes with 'überzeugt': 'fest davon überzeugt' means firmly convinced of it.
Add '-in' to a job noun to make it female: 'Gärtner' becomes 'Gärtnerin', a female gardener.
The verb 'heißen' means to be called, so 'Ich heiße Anna' is literally I am called Anna, the normal way to give your name.
To say you like doing something, add 'gern' to the verb: 'trinkt gern' means likes to drink.
'Neugierig auf' takes the accusative – curious about something, as in 'neugierig auf das Ergebnis'.
The phrase 'zufrieden mit' means satisfied with, and 'mit' always takes the dative: 'mit dem Ergebnis'.
The word 'dass' sends the verb to the end of its clause: 'dass das stimmt', with 'stimmt' last.
The diminutive ending '-chen' always makes a noun neuter: 'das Glühwürmchen', even though a 'Wurm' is masculine.
The words 'weder' and 'noch' work as a pair meaning neither and nor: 'weder Fisch noch Fleisch'.
Comparatives add '-er' and use 'als' for than: 'schwieriger als erwartet', more difficult than expected.
With 'seit' for ongoing time, German uses the present tense where English uses have been: 'seit fünfzehn Jahren'.
The preposition 'auf' takes the dative when it marks location without movement: 'liegt auf dem Küchentisch'.
With a time, 'erst' means not until: 'öffnet erst Mitte Mai' means it opens no sooner than mid-May.
The verb stays in second position: 'normalerweise' fills the first slot, so 'frühstücke' comes right after it.
'Stolz auf' always takes the accusative – proud of someone or something: 'stolz auf unsere Tochter'.
German uses 'machen', to make, for earning a license: 'den Führerschein machen' means to pass your driving test.
German says allergic against, not to: 'allergisch gegen Nüsse und Erdbeeren'.
'Die Katze' is feminine – nouns ending in '-e' are often feminine.
With a clock time, 'gegen' means around, not against: 'gegen elf Uhr' is about eleven o'clock.
The verb 'erklären' gives the person the dative, 'dem Schüler', while the thing explained stays accusative.
